To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the genotype of S. enterica Enteritidis strains is correlated to the phenotype, but the differences between strains are minor, rather than the major differences that would be expected if the strains differed in virulence or in the ability to cause egg contamination.

the genotype of Salmonella Enteritidis is correlated with its phenotype, and that the phenotype is correlated with its ability to cause foodborne salmonellosis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a molecular understanding of the mechanisms of egg contamination by Salmonella enterica, which has resulted in a significant public health problem.
understanding the genetic basis for phenotypic differences among S. enterica strains that are associated with egg contamination.
understanding the molecular basis for the emergence of S. enterica as an important foodborne pathogen.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the genotype of a strain of S. enterica subsp. enterica serotype Enteritidis does not always correlate with the phenotype of that strain.
the phenotypes of S. enterica subsp. enterica serotypes are more likely to be influenced by the genetic changes in the host cell than by changes in the lysogenic bacteriophages.
there is no evidence that the genotype of S. enterica subsp. enterica serogroup D, serovar Enteriditis is associated with a specific phenotype.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
S. enteritidis is a complex of strains that are genetically similar but phenotypically different and that the different strains have different abilities to grow in the egg.
the phenotype of the bacteria is a reflection of the genotype of the bacteria.
the genotype of the bacteria is not always the best predictor of phenotype, and the phenotype is not always the predictor of the genotype.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the genomic changes in S. enterica are not necessarily the cause of the phenotypic changes that affect food safety.
it is important to understand that the phenotype of a bacterium is a function of the environment and not the genotype.
the genomic differences between S. enterica subsp. enterica serotype Enteritidis PT 4 and 13A are subtle and do not account for the different phenotypes.
